notes.1a: Many correct answers were seen here. The most common errors were either omitting the hundredths of a second in the calculation or not converting to seconds.
notes.1b: A considerable number of candidates correctly indicated that the stopwatch should be started when the LED flashed. Many did not fully understand that the period between two flashes was too brief to measure with accuracy. The time interval for a large number of flashes needed to be found.
notes.2a: This part was answered well, many candidates showed both the correct equation and full working. Weaker candidates often used an incorrect equation i.e. speed = distance x time.
notes.2b: (i) Many candidates understood that the distance travelled was equal to the area under the graph and also applied this knowledge successfully. A common error was omitting the ½ when calculating the area of the triangle.
notes.2bii: This was answered very well, with most candidates gaining full credit.
notes.2c: Most candidates attempted this part and many got the correct answer. A common error was to divide the mass by 10 instead of multiplying by 10.
notes.3a: (i) Most candidates knew that the model aircraft would continue moving forwards. Common errors were giving the size of the resultant force either as 30N or 19N.
notes.3aii: Again most candidates knew that the model aircraft would continue moving forwards. The effect of this resultant force on the aircraft’s speed (i.e. the aircraft accelerates or speed increases) was not always understood.
notes.3b: Few candidates understood that either air resistance increasing with speed or a reduction in thrust would enable the horizontal forces to balance. A common error was to state that the aircraft would stop when there was no resultant horizontal force acting on it.
notes.4a: (i) A common incorrect answer was kinetic energy. The bag is moving, so it does have kinetic energy; however, it does not gain kinetic energy because ‘it is lifted at constant speed.’
notes.4aii: This part was answered well by most candidates.
notes.4iii: Many candidates realised that the height raised was required but there was a lack of knowledge that the time was also needed.
notes.4b: The majority of candidates gained full credit on this part.
notes.5a: This was well answered by the majority of candidates.
notes.5b: Candidates did not fully understand the process of evaporation. Few correct marking points were seen, usually only for the idea that energy transfers from the water to the liquid.
notes.6a: (i) Very few candidates understood that a point on a transverse wave moves at right angles to the wave direction. Many candidates gave no response to this question.
notes.6aii: Many correct answers were seen, but a common error was to give the total length of all four waves.
notes.6iii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.6b: (i) Candidates tended to select sound or just radio, and very few selected light and radio.
notes.6bii: Most answers given were correct with many candidates giving sound as their answer. There were a significant number of no response answers.
notes.7a: Many candidates gave the correct answer for the unit of temperature. The physical property was more challenging for some candidates. Common errors were: length, mercury, boiling or freezing but many candidates gave no response.
notes.7b: Most answers given were correct. A common error was the omission of the unit after the 0 and 100. There were a significant number of no response answers.
notes.8a: Many answers focused on a process, reflection or refraction, rather than just stating the term, normal.
notes.8b: Candidates needed to understand that the required angles were the angles between the ray and the normal. In addition, the direction of the ray needed to be considered. There was also some confusion between reflection and refraction.
notes.8c: Most candidates knew the effect was refraction but few were able to explain why refraction occurred and many gave no response.
notes.9a: (i),(ii) The majority of candidates understood the arrangement of the magnetic poles for this effect but fewer were able to recall the term, repulsion.
notes.9aiii: Many candidates gave a correct description of what would happen. The term ‘attract’ was not always used.
notes.9b: (i),(ii) There was considerable confusion between electrostatic charge and magnetism in many answers. Only the strongest candidates gained any credit on this question.
notes.9biii: When answered, responses were often too vague e.g. to attract an object, to pick objects up.
notes.10a: This part was answered well but variable resistor or just resistor were common errors.
notes.10b: (i) The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.10bii: Many correct answers were seen for this calculation and these often showed both the correct equation and full working. Weaker candidates were unable to rearrange the V = I × R equation and used the incorrect I = V × R. (0.015 A)
notes.11a: (i) Many of the answers seen merely stated that d.c. was the abbreviation for direct current instead of explaining its meaning.
notes.11aii: Few correct answers were seen. The two cells were often drawn in parallel and candidates did not seem to know the symbol for a switch.
notes.11b: (i) Very few correct answers were seen and transformer was a popular incorrect answer.
notes.11bii: A number of candidates gained partial credit here, usually for “increasing the current”. A common error was to suggest using bigger magnets instead of stronger or more powerful magnets.
notes.12a: (i),(ii) The majority of answers were correct.
notes.12b: Many of the answers seen were correct. Common errors were the Sun and/or listing regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.
notes.12c: A number of candidates gained some credit here, usually for the knowledge that when electrons are gained, the atom becomes negatively charged.
notes.12d: The majority of the answers seen were correct. There was no particular error pattern.
notes.key_messages:
• Candidates should note both the number of marks available and the space allocated for responses,
as these factors provide a clear indication of the type of answer expected. For example, for a two-
mark question, two distinct points should be given.
• In calculations, candidates should set out and explain their working clearly. Credit may be given for
correct working even if the final answer is incorrect.
• Before starting their response, candidates are advised to read the question carefully, paying
attention to the command words, to ensure they focus their answers as required.
notes.general_comments:
For many candidates the non-numerical questions were more of a challenge than numerical questions.
Some areas of the syllabus were better known than others. In particular, evaporation, general wave
properties, magnetism, electric circuits, electromagnetics and radioactivity were not well understood.
Equations were generally well known by all but the weakest candidates. Many candidates understood how to
apply equations to fairly standard situations well.
A noticeable number of candidates struggled to express themselves adequately.
